data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Sandbags and floods are physical and uncorrelated except under the extreme event, whereas decentralized services can be synchronized by minor signals (market prices) long before the extreme event.","A large service can dynamically allocate internal redundancy, whereas a sandbag's capacity is static."],"overturn_conditions":["Evidence that decentralized networks can reorganize and heal during an extreme event faster than the event propagates.","Proof that the large service's concentrated redundancy introduces a single point of failure that makes it MORE vulnerable to extreme events than distributed small services."],"shared_structure":["Both a decentralized network and a row of individual sandbags appear resilient to moderate stress, but both fail simultaneously under an extreme flood that exceeds their individual capacities.","Both a large service and a single, massive levee concentrate redundancy to withstand a greater magnitude of the same extreme flood."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_004"],"transfer_claims":["If a row of sandbags washes away together in a 100-year flood while a single large levee holds, a decentralized network will fail together in a massive outage while a large service survives.","The apparent independence of the sandbags is an observer bias; their true correlation is revealed only under extreme stress."]},"claim":"The claim is false: the apparent resilience of a decentralized network is an artifact of observer bias, because extreme value statistics ensure that any shared cause capable of affecting the small services will inevitably destroy them, making the large service with its internal redundancy strictly superior.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The large service's redundancy is concentrated in a single physical location, making it vulnerable to a localized physical event that would spare a geographically distributed decentralized network.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The shared causes are drawn from a distribution with bounded support, meaning extreme events do not scale to overcome the small services' redundancy.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The small services are geographically and topologically diverse, meaning a large shared cause cannot physically reach all of them simultaneously.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Observers mistakenly model the survival of decentralized networks as evidence of independence. However, shared causes that can overcome the redundancy of a small service are extreme events (e.g., massive DDoS, cloud provider outage, critical DNS failure). By the statistics of extremes, if such an event is large enough to breach one small service's redundancy, it is large enough to breach all of them simultaneously. The large service, having strictly more internal redundancy, raises the threshold of breach. The small services appear uncorrelated until a sufficiently large shared cause arrives, at which point they fail in perfect synchrony. The large service is therefore strictly more resilient because its redundancy is additive and concentrated against the tail event.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
